title: Quantum antidipolar systems in two-dimensional geometries
abstract: Particles with magnetic moment can be polarized, and rapidly rotated, employing a magnetic field such that the dipolar interaction among them changes sign, becoming antidipolar and thus isotropically attractive in a plane. Polar molecules can also be manipulated using microwave dressing fields to invert the sign of the dipole-dipole interaction. In this work, we study a two-dimensional system of antidipolar particles by calculating its equation of state and structural properties. The system behaves as a liquid even for scattering lengths significantly greater than the dipolar length. For large enough densities, the system transitions to a solid with one particle per lattice site via a first-order phase transition at a significantly smaller density than its dipolar counterpart. Moreover, motivated by the recent realization of a strongly axially trapped, bilayer geometry [Science 384, 546-551 (2024)], we study the properties of the bilayer liquid phase as the inter-layer distance is tuned, and provide the range of parameters where one layer can influence the properties of the other.
summary: This paper theoretically investigates quantum antidipolar systems in 2D, analyzing both single-layer and bilayer geometries. It calculates the equation of state and structural properties, finding that the system undergoes a first-order liquid-solid transition. Furthermore, it details how tuning the inter-layer separation allows one layer to significantly influence the superfluidity and energy of the other layer.
main_problem: The study investigates the properties of two-dimensional (2D) quantum systems interacting via antidipolar forces, examining single-layer and bilayer configurations.
main_result: The system exhibits liquid-solid phase transitions at lower densities than expected for standard dipolar systems, and the bilayer structure shows tunable inter-layer coupling effects on superfluidity and energy.
method: The research employs advanced quantum many-body techniques, including Diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) and the calculation of expectation values using Jastrow-Slater trial wave functions.
model_or_system: The model consists of particles with tunable antidipolar interactions, confined to 2D planes, potentially forming a bilayer structure. The Hamiltonian includes terms for intra-layer and inter-layer dipole-dipole interactions.
key_observables: Equation of state (EOS), structural properties, liquid-solid transition points, superfluid fraction ($f_s$), and condensate fraction ($f_c$).
important_parameters: Inter-layer distance ($h$), interaction strength ratio ($C_{12}/(E_0r_{12}^0)$), and particle density ($n$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on approximations like the Feynman approximation for excitation spectra and assumes the system can be described by specific Jastrow-type trial wave functions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate simulation snapshots of liquid and solid phases, the inter-particle potential, the energy per particle vs. density for the bilayer, and the superfluid/condensate fractions vs. inter-layer distance.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the single-layer liquid-solid transition, then extending the analysis to the bilayer geometry to study how tuning the inter-layer distance modifies the system's thermodynamic and superfluid properties.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the complex physics of dipolar quantum gases in reduced dimensions, which is a major frontier in AMO physics, particularly concerning phase transitions and interlayer coupling.
